records.quote: Theorem 4: Let Y ~ EIPLD(alpha_1, beta_1, theta_1) and Z ~ EIPLD(alpha_2, beta_2, theta_2). If beta_1 = beta_2 and theta_2 >= theta_1 (or if beta_2 >= beta_1 and theta_1 = theta_2) then (Y <=lr Z) for all z. ... Setting alpha_1 = alpha_2. Case 1: for beta_1 = beta_2 and theta_2 >= theta_1 we obtained d/dz [g_Z(z)/g_Y(z)] as an increasing function of z. Case 2: beta_2 >= beta_1 and theta_1 = theta_2 we obtained d/dz [g_Z(z)/g_Y(z)] as an increasing function of z. This implies that Y <=lr Z for all z. Hence Y <=hr Z, Y <=mrl Z and Y <=st Z.

note: Theorem 4 proves Y <=lr Z (under alpha_1=alpha_2 plus either parameter case) and then states 'Hence Y <=hr Z, Y <=mrl Z and Y <=st Z' — four named orders, so four records. Pass B bundled all into one lr record.

The Section 8 block restates standard order definitions and the textbook implication chain lr => hr => mrl => st (attributed to Shaked and Shanthikumar 1994); it is a definitions passage, not a theorem/proposition/example making a claim about two model distributions.
